case_study_insert.main_stem: Northern Rails Freight (NRF) is a private limited company in the rail freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2011 by Anika Northern, the business hauls bulk containers for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NRF plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new diesel-electric shunting fleet and a regional depot, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $28, and handles 40,000 units of freight a year. NRF faces two problems: wagon turnaround delays have pushed late deliveries to 14%, and a diesel-maintenance skills gap is raising repair costs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Report, Q4 2025: NRF moved 10,400 container units last quarter, with a late-delivery rate of 14%, down from 18% a year earlier. Damage claims fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average wagon turnaround is 2.6 days. A survey of 400 manufacturing clients found 71% would pay a 5% premium for guaranteed overnight slots, and 48% rank reliability above price. A skills audit shows 26 of 120 drivers lack diesel-engine maintenance certification; accredited courses cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northern Rails Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising interest costs on NRF's $700,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour from April 2026, increasing the wage bill for NRF's 120 staff. (3) Diesel fuel input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year while economy-wide inflation is 4.2%; freight contract rates in NRF's region grew only 2.1%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for NRF of financing its $1,200,000 depot expansion with retained profit instead of the $700,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $500,000 retained profit costs NRF no interest or capital repayment, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year and a $700,000 loan commitment. With late deliveries at 14% and repair costs rising because of the diesel-maintenance skills gap, keeping interest charges low leaves more cash to fund training and shunting-fleet reliability. Every dollar not paid to the lender supports the $28 selling price and the $10 contribution without passing costs on to the 400 manufacturing clients.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the $1,200,000 depot and new shunting fleet are not jeopardised if freight demand falls short of the 40,000-unit target. It also preserves Anika Northern's ownership and control: no external lender can impose conditions on how the regional depot is run or on the guaranteed overnight-slot strategy. That freedom lets NRF respond quickly to the 71% of surveyed clients who would pay a premium for guaranteed slots, which a lender imposing repayment milestones might restrict.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to NRF's expansion, costs and survey data.

questions.question_text: NRF is promoting its new guaranteed overnight freight slots. Consider national rail trade press advertising, regional radio sponsorship, or a direct email campaign to its 400 surveyed manufacturing clients. Which should NRF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National rail trade press advertising: A campaign in rail and logistics trade titles would build credibility with the manufacturers who already buy NRF's bulk container haulage, and print adverts can explain the technical detail of guaranteed overnight slots. The downside is slow response and high cost relative to a business with fixed costs of $320,000 a year and a $700,000 loan to service; readership is also national while NRF serves a regional depot catchment, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio sponsorship: Radio reaches local manufacturers cheaply and quickly, and repeated slogans suit a simple message about reliability, which matters because 48% of surveyed clients rank reliability above price. However, radio cannot demonstrate the overnight guarantee and its audience includes many listeners who never buy freight services, so the 71% of the 400 surveyed clients who would pay a premium are not efficiently isolated.

Direct email campaign: A targeted email to the 400 manufacturing clients in NRF's own database reaches exactly the buyers who already use its services, can quote the 5% premium finding back to them, and costs little per contact. It is measurable through opens and replies, and can be personalised by depot. Its limits are that it cannot win entirely new customers and inboxes are crowded, so the message must be sharp.

Recommendation: NRF should choose the direct email campaign. It targets the precise segment in its own research, costs far less than trade press, and reaches the 71% willing to pay a premium, while radio and press are rejected as untargeted and expensive for a business funding an $1,200,000 expansion. NRF should add small trade-press adverts later to build awareness.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to NRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NRF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation that explains why trade press and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: NRF's late deliveries have reached 14% and a diesel-maintenance skills gap is raising repair costs. Explain two benefits for NRF of using autocratic leadership to improve performance in its depot.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Anika Northern set clear, uniform turnaround procedures across the hierarchical structure, so crane and shunting crews follow one agreed routine rather than local shortcuts. With wagon turnaround currently 2.6 days and late deliveries at 14%, a single imposed standard and close supervision can cut delays quickly, protecting the 40,000-unit service commitment and the 400 manufacturing clients who value reliability.

Point 2: Decisive, top-down instructions speed up the response to the diesel-maintenance skills gap. The audit shows 26 of 120 drivers lack certification, and autocratic leadership can immediately allocate the $1,100-per-employee accredited courses and enforce attendance without lengthy consultation. Faster decisions also mean breakdowns are triaged quickly, repairing wagons before they worsen the 14% late-delivery figure and keeping repair costs from eroding the $10 contribution per unit. A consultative approach would slow these decisions, whereas a clear directive keeps the 400 manufacturing clients confident that NRF can recover from the 14% late-delivery problem quickly.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to NRF's delivery, skills and cost data.

questions.question_text: NRF must close a diesel-engine maintenance skills gap among 26 of its 120 staff. Consider in-house on-the-job coaching or accredited off-the-job courses costing $1,100 per employee. Which should NRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house on-the-job coaching: Coaching in NRF's own depot uses the actual diesel-electric shunting fleet and maintenance routines, so skills transfer directly and staff keep working while they learn, which protects the 40,000-unit service and helps attack the 14% late-delivery rate. It avoids course fees and can be delivered by the most experienced fitters. Weaknesses are that it depends on those fitters' availability, can pass on bad habits, and gives no external certificate, which may matter if manufacturers audit NRF's maintenance standards.

Accredited off-the-job courses: Paying $1,100 per employee gives all 26 staff a recognised qualification and up-to-date diesel-engine knowledge. The total cost of 26 × $1,100 = $28,600 is small beside the $1,200,000 depot investment and could be met from the $500,000 retained profit. The drawback is that 26 of 120 staff are away from the depot during training, reducing capacity at a time when turnaround averages 2.6 days and late deliveries already stand at 14%; the generic syllabus may also need follow-up on NRF's own wagons.

Decision: NRF should choose accredited off-the-job courses, followed by short on-site coaching. The $28,600 cost is affordable and the certificate directly addresses the audit finding on 26 unqualified drivers, whereas on-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it would perpetuate existing habits and offer no proof of competence to clients. Capacity loss can be spread across shifts, so the short-term disruption is manageable. Phasing the courses across small groups would limit that loss further, and the certificate would help NRF demonstrate competence to the 400 manufacturing clients when they audit the regional depot.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to NRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in NRF's context, with some cost awareness.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both options using the 26 staff, $1,100 and $28,600 figures, with a justified decision explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $320,000 ÷ ($28 − $18) = $320,000 ÷ $10 = 32,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 32,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28 − $18 = $10. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NRF's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 32,000-unit break-even point with actual volume of 40,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 8,000 units, so managers can see how far volumes could fall before the regional depot loses money.
2. Use the $10 contribution to test the 5% premium mentioned by 71% of surveyed clients: a higher effective price would raise contribution and lower break-even, informing the overnight-slot pricing decision.
3. Assess whether the $700,000 bank loan and the $1,200,000 investment can be serviced by checking that output above 32,000 units generates enough contribution to cover the $320,000 fixed costs and interest payable.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $26 a unit ($320,000 ÷ 40,000 + $18) each quarter to spot the repair costs caused by the diesel-maintenance skills gap and to judge supplier negotiations as diesel input costs rise 9.5%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 32,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 8,000 units against 40,000 output; premium pricing from the 71% survey finding; loan-service feasibility on the $700,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $26 to track maintenance costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NRF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NRF's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 37.5%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $3,000,000 divided by revenue of $8,000,000 gives 37.5%; 2025 gross profit of $3,600,000 divided by $9,000,000 gives 40.0%. Operating profit of $1,000,000 divided by 2024 revenue gives 12.5%; 2025 operating profit of $1,350,000 divided by $9,000,000 gives 15.0%. Return on capital employed of $1,000,000 on $5,000,000 capital gives 20.0%; 2025 return of $1,350,000 on $6,000,000 gives 22.5%. Revenue grew 12.5% while cost of sales grew only 8.0%, and operating profit rose 35% against a 20% rise in capital employed.

Evaluation: Both years show a clear upward trend. The gross margin widened from 37.5% to 40.0% because revenue outpaced cost of sales, suggesting better control over diesel and maintenance spending even as the 14% late-delivery problem persisted. Operating return rose from 12.5% to 15.0%, so overheads were absorbed more effectively. Returns on the expanded capital base also improved, from 20.0% to 22.5%, which is important because the $1,200,000 depot and shunting fleet must justify the $700,000 loan. Interest payable rose from $120,000 to $150,000, but operating profit still grew far faster, so borrowing to fund expansion did not dent returns. A caveat is that these figures are historic and do not capture the 9.5% diesel increase in Appendix 3.

Conclusion: NRF's profitability has improved on all three measures, and the improvement is genuine because it is not dependent on a one-off asset sale. The main risk is that rising diesel input costs could squeeze the 40.0% gross margin in the next year, so management should protect the $10 contribution per unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or trends with little or no accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with some relevant analysis of the trends.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NRF of offering guaranteed overnight freight slots to its manufacturing clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 400 manufacturing clients found that 71% would pay a 5% premium for guaranteed overnight slots and that 48% rank reliability above price, so NRF can raise its effective price above the $28 selling price and increase the $10 contribution per unit. This directly attacks the 14% late-delivery problem by making punctuality a sellable feature, helping win business from competitors and strengthening the case for the $1,200,000 depot investment.

Disadvantage: A genuine overnight guarantee demands extra wagons, drivers and tight wagon turnaround, pushing up the $320,000 fixed costs and possibly the $18 variable cost per unit through overtime or premium fuel. If NRF misses a slot, the 71% who paid the premium may claim compensation, damaging the reliability reputation the service is meant to build. With a $700,000 bank loan already being serviced, any extra operating cost could erase the gain from the 5% premium before the new shunting fleet is fully productive.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed development using NRF's survey, cost and delivery data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% diesel cost rise will affect NRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If NRF's $700,000 loan is variable-rate, the interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points, shown as 0.0075 × $700,000 = $5,250 a year. That is modest against fixed costs of $320,000 and interest payable of $150,000 in the accounts, and it could be removed by fixing the loan rate. It may also make future borrowing dearer, but it is a one-off financing effect rather than a continuing hit on every unit.

Minimum wage increase (5.8% to $13.75): The insert states a workforce of 120 and output of 40,000 units, so labour productivity is 40,000 ÷ 120 = 333.3 units per worker. Hours worked and individual pay are not given, so a wage-bill total cannot be invented; the honest test is whether productivity holds near 333 units or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $10 contribution shrinks. The effect is real but manageable if the 26 staff are trained and turnaround improves.

Diesel cost rise (9.5%): The insert does not split the $18 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if all of it were fuel, 9.5% × $18 = $1.71 per unit, and at 40,000 units that is 40,000 × $1.71 = $68,400 a year. Even a smaller fuel share would cut the $10 contribution, and freight contract rates grew only 2.1%, so NRF cannot easily pass the rise on.

Conclusion: The 9.5% diesel increase will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 40,000 units, directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,200,000 expansion, and is harder to neutralise than the $5,250 interest rise or a wage increase that productivity can offset. The wage rise is second because it is a large recurring cost, while the interest rise is smallest and can be hedged.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NRF's costs or financing using case figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown arithmetic, a justified greatest-impact judgement on diesel costs, and reasons why the other two are smaller.
